lesson.title: Read an IPv4 prefix boundary
lesson.summary: Calculate one IPv4 block and distinguish its address count from conventional LAN host capacity.
lesson.explanation:
An IPv4 address has 32 bits. A /26 fixes the first 26 bits and leaves six varying bits. Those six bits represent 64 combinations. The prefix selects an aligned block; it is not a count of available devices.

For a conventional broadcast subnet, reserve the all-zero and all-one host patterns for the network and broadcast addresses. Point-to-point /31 links are a separate case; do not apply the subtract-two rule to every prefix.
lesson.why: A correct block boundary prevents allocating addresses in the wrong subnet or confusing routing with host capacity.
lesson.example: For 192.168.10.42/26, blocks in the last octet begin at 0, 64, 128 and 192. The address 42 falls in the first block. Network: 192.168.10.0. Upper address: 192.168.10.63. Total: 64; conventional LAN host addresses: .1 through .62.
lesson.takeaway: First find the aligned address block; then apply the rules for how that block is used.
objectives: Find the network and upper address for a /26.
Explain why 64 addresses and 62 conventional hosts are different quantities.
lesson.misconception: Subtracting two is not a universal IPv4 formula: /31 point-to-point links have different address semantics.

quiz.q: For 192.168.10.70/26, which block contains the address?
quiz.explanation: A /26 spans 64 aligned addresses. 70 lies in the block starting at 64 and ending at 127. Starting a block at the host value ignores alignment; 126 omits the upper address.

verification.method: Prefix arithmetic checked against the current browser calculator and RFC 4632 §3.1; editorial signoff required before publication.

teachingPackEntry.essentialQuestion: How can 192.168.10.42/26 identify a 64-address block rather than 42 devices?
teachingPackEntry.verifiedBoundary: The prefix fixes the leading bits; six varying bits produce 64 addresses.
teachingPackEntry.analogy: A row of 64 numbered mailboxes helps picture an aligned block, but mailbox labels are an analogy, not a routing protocol.

starter.plainStart: Find the block containing the address, then count its members.
starter.tryThis: Before calculating, decide whether .70 belongs with .42.

technical.scope: The calculator reports conventional LAN counts for /0–/30, point-to-point endpoint counts for /31, and a single address for /32. It does not allocate addresses or configure a network.
technical.versionCaution: Check platform address reservations before operational use.

reasoningSteps: Set the host bits to zero for the network and to one for the upper address.
Separate total addresses from the usage-specific host count.
Check a second address and explain why the boundary moved.
memoryLadder: Explain prefix length without the calculator.
Explain why .63 and .64 fall on opposite sides of a boundary.
Teach the difference between address count and host count.
labPlan: Enter 192.168.10.42 and prefix 26. Write your prediction in the saved working notes.
Calculate. Expect network 192.168.10.0/26, upper address .63, 64 total and 62 conventional hosts.
Change only the address to .70; expect network .64 and upper address .127.
Change only the prefix to 27; predict the smaller block before calculating.
Enter 10..0.1 or prefix 1.5. Explain why validation rejects it rather than displaying the previous answer.
Use Reset model to restore .42/26. Compare the two cases in your notes, answer the quiz and schedule a review.

vocabulary.definition: The number of leading address bits fixed by the prefix.
The remaining address bits that vary within the block.
A block starts at a multiple of its size within the address space.
